Module 03 / Physics 2

Electric charge and force: signs before substitution

Charging, Coulomb forces, vectors, and source-label corrections.

Topics in this module
Quantization, conservation, and charging mechanismsCoulomb's law: empirical starting law and algebraic formsSuperposition in one, two, and three dimensionsRectangles, diagonals, and force cancellationCharging diagrams and charge-conservation calculationsComplete the source force problems in one and two dimensionsSituational problems: choose the law, then solve

Charge is a property of matter, not a synonym for “electron.” Electrons carry −e, protons +e, and neutrons zero net charge. Use e=1.602×10−19 Ce = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}e=1.602×10−19C in course calculations. A positive net charge usually indicates an electron deficit. A negative net charge indicates excess electrons. Ordinary rubbing transfers electrons rather than creating charge.

Quantization, conservation, and charging mechanisms

q=(Np−Ne)e,N=∣q∣e,Δm=Nme.q=(N_p-N_e)e,\quad N=\frac{|q|}{e},\quad \Delta m=N m_e.q=(Np​−Ne​)e,N=e∣q∣​,Δm=Nme​.

For ordinary isolated charged bodies, q is an integer multiple of e. An isolated system conserves total signed charge: ∑qbefore=∑qafter\sum q_{\mathrm{before}} = \sum q_{\mathrm{after}}∑qbefore​=∑qafter​. Neutral means balanced net charge, not absence of charged particles. Charge is frame invariant in the classical situations covered here.

Worked example — primary p. 8. A charge of +0.32 C+ 0.32\,\mathrm{C}+0.32C represents 0.32(1.602×10−19)=1.998×1018\frac{0.32}{\left( 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \right)} = 1.998 \times 10^{18}(1.602×10−19)0.32​=1.998×1018 removed electrons. Its mass decreases by about 1.82×10−12 kg1.82 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}1.82×10−12kg if only electron transfer changes its mass. Neutrino oscillations show that neutrinos are not all massless. The source's blanket zero-rest-mass statement is inaccurate and unnecessary for this charge calculation.

Conduction requires contact and permits charge transfer. Friction transfers charge during rubbing. Induction separates charge without contact with the inducing body. To leave a single conductor with net charge by the standard grounding method, approach the charged rod, connect the ground, remove the ground, then remove the rod. Changing that order can remove the intended final charge. Polarization separates positive and negative charge slightly within a neutral object; attraction does not prove the object has acquired a net charge.

Conductors have mobile charges. Insulators restrict bulk charge motion. Semiconductors have conductivity between these broad categories and strongly depend on material conditions. In electrostatic equilibrium, excess conductor charge lies on its surface; the field inside conducting material is zero. These statements concern equilibrium, not every current-carrying wire.

Coulomb's law: empirical starting law and algebraic forms

For stationary point charges in vacuum, use k≈8.99×109 N⋅m2C2k \approx \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{N} \cdot m^{2}}{C^{2}}k≈C28.99×109N⋅m2​. Coulomb's inverse-square law is an empirical starting law here; it cannot be independently proved just by rearranging its definition.

F=k∣q1q2∣r2,r=k∣q1q2∣F,∣q1∣=Fr2k∣q2∣.F=k\frac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2},\quad r=\sqrt{\frac{k|q_1q_2|}{F}},\quad |q_1|=\frac{Fr^2}{k|q_2|}.F=kr2∣q1​q2​∣​,r=Fk∣q1​q2​∣​​,∣q1​∣=k∣q2​∣Fr2​.

Use magnitudes in this scalar formula. Determine attraction or repulsion separately. Like signs repel; opposite signs attract. Doubling r divides F by four. Tripling one charge triples F. In a uniform linear medium with relative permittivity κ\kappaκ, replace ε0\varepsilon_{0}ε0​ by κε0\kappa \varepsilon_{0}κε0​ if the problem justifies that model.

Worked example — primary p. 22. q1=+25 nCq_{1} = + 25\,\mathrm{nC}q1​=+25nC, q2=−75 nCq_{2} = - 75\,\mathrm{nC}q2​=−75nC, r=3.0 cm=0.030 mr = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.030\,\mathrm{m}r=3.0cm=0.030m. F=(8.99×109)(25×10−9)(75×10−9)(0.030)2=0.01873 N\begin{aligned}F &= \frac{\left( 8.99 \times 10^{9} \right) \left( 25 \times 10^{-9} \right) \left( 75 \times 10^{-9} \right)}{\left( 0.030 \right)^{2}} \\&= 0.01873\,\mathrm{N}\end{aligned}F​=(0.030)2(8.99×109)(25×10−9)(75×10−9)​=0.01873N​ Both forces have this magnitude. Their directions are opposite and attractive. A larger charge does not experience the larger force in this two-body pair.

Rectangles, diagonals, and force cancellation

For the rectangular arrangement in primary pp. 26–28, draw all forces on the SAME corner charge. A 3–4–5 rectangle has diagonal r=5r = 5r=5 units. A diagonal force's component factors are 45\frac{4}{5}54​ and 35\frac{3}{5}53​ when the horizontal side is 4 units. The diagonal force is 230.4 μN230.4\,\mathrm{\mu N}230.4μN with k=9×109k = 9 \times 10^{9}k=9×109. Its magnitude does not decide its component signs. The complete solution below corrects the previous factor-of-ten error in these notes.

The source's working mixes a downward −90° direction with a positive j term. Recompute from the arrows instead of copying that sign. If a diagonal force points upper-left, its components are (−4F5- \frac{4 F}{5}−54F​, +3F5+ \frac{3 F}{5}+53F​). Add the horizontal and vertical forces algebraically after resolving the diagonal.

For two like-signed sources on a line, a cancellation point lies between them. For opposite signs, their fields reinforce between them; a possible zero-field point lies outside on the smaller-magnitude charge's side. Solve in each physically allowed region. Squaring distance equations can produce an invalid location.

Derive the cancellation location. Put positive Q1Q_{1}Q1​ at x=0x = 0x=0 and positive Q2Q_{2}Q2​ at x=dx = dx=d. A nonzero test charge between them has opposing forces. Cancel its magnitude and k: Q1x2=Q2(d−x)2\frac{Q_{1}}{x^{2}} = \frac{Q_{2}}{\left( d - x \right)^{2}}x2Q1​​=(d−x)2Q2​​. Both distances are positive in this region. Taking positive square roots and collecting x gives:

Q1(d−x)=Q2x⇒x=dQ1Q1+Q2.\sqrt{Q_1}(d-x)=\sqrt{Q_2}x\Rightarrow x=\frac{d\sqrt{Q_1}}{\sqrt{Q_1}+\sqrt{Q_2}}.Q1​​(d−x)=Q2​​x⇒x=Q1​​+Q2​​dQ1​​​.

For +4 nC+ 4\,\mathrm{nC}+4nC and +9 nC+ 9\,\mathrm{nC}+9nC separated by 1.00 m1.00\,\mathrm{m}1.00m, x=2(2+3)=0.400 mx = \frac{2}{\left( 2 + 3 \right)} = 0.400\,\mathrm{m}x=(2+3)2​=0.400m from +4 nC+ 4\,\mathrm{nC}+4nC. The fields there have equal magnitudes and opposite directions. The point is closer to the smaller charge because its weaker source needs a smaller distance to match the other field.

Opposite-sign extension. Put +4 nC+ 4\,\mathrm{nC}+4nC at x=0x = 0x=0 and −9 nC- 9\,\mathrm{nC}−9nC at x=1.00 mx = 1.00\,\mathrm{m}x=1.00m. Between them, both fields point right. Test x<0x < 0x<0 instead: 4x2=9(1−x)2\frac{4}{x^{2}} = \frac{9}{\left( 1 - x \right)^{2}}x24​=(1−x)29​. Positive distances give 2(1−x)=3(−x)2 \left( 1 - x \right) = 3 \left( - x \right)2(1−x)=3(−x), so x=−2.00 mx = - 2.00\,\mathrm{m}x=−2.00m. Substitution gives equal field magnitudes 8.99 NC8.99\,\frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}8.99CN​, with opposite directions. Equal opposite charges have no finite zero-field point on their joining line.

Source problems · full working

Charging diagrams and charge-conservation calculations

Names and signs — primary pp. 4–6. The historical word “electric” comes from the Greek word for amber. The coulomb names the charge unit after Coulomb. Franklin's positive and negative labels distinguish the two charge signs. “Positive” does not mean more electrons; an electron deficit gives a positive net charge in the ordinary charging examples.

Particle Approximate mass, kg Charge, C
Electron 9.11×10−319.11 \times 10^{-31}9.11×10−31 −1.602×10−19- 1.602 \times 10^{-19}−1.602×10−19
Proton 1.673×10−271.673 \times 10^{-27}1.673×10−27 +1.602×10−19+ 1.602 \times 10^{-19}+1.602×10−19
Neutron 1.675×10−271.675 \times 10^{-27}1.675×10−27 0

Source correction. Primary p. 21 repeats the proton's mass for the neutron. Their masses are close but not identical. The rounded values above distinguish them. A neutral object can contain many charged particles; their net charge cancels.

Grounding. Earth acts as a large charge reservoir. Connecting a conductor to ground lets electrons move as the surrounding electric field requires. With a nearby negative rod, electrons leave the grounded conductor. Remove the ground first, then the rod: the conductor remains positive. A positive inducing rod draws electrons from ground and leaves the conductor negative after the same removal sequence.

Conduction versus polarization. A charged metal redistributes mobile electrons over its surface. Charge on an insulating rod does not spread as freely. Neutral paper can still be attracted to a charged comb. Polarization places the nearer opposite-sign charge slightly closer, making its attraction exceed the farther like-sign repulsion. Attraction alone does not prove a net charge.

Count the transferred electrons and check the charge sign

Source: Primary p. 8. Given: Initially neutral body; final charge +0.32 C+ 0.32\,\mathrm{C}+0.32C; e=1.602×10−19 Ce = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}e=1.602×10−19C.

  1. Identify an electron deficit because the final charge is positive.
  2. Use N=∣Q∣eN = \frac{\left| Q \right|}{e}N=e∣Q∣​, with both quantities in coulombs.
  3. Calculate N=0.32(1.602×10−19)=1.99750×1018N = \frac{0.32}{\left( 1.602 \times 10^{-19} \right)} = 1.99750 \times 10^{18}N=(1.602×10−19)0.32​=1.99750×1018 electrons removed.
  4. Check the sign: removing negative charge produces a positive change in net charge.
  5. If asked for mass change, use Δm=−Nme\Delta m = - Nm_{e}Δm=−Nme​. With me=9.11×10−31 kgm_{e} = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}me​=9.11×10−31kg, Δm≈−1.82×10−12 kg\Delta m \approx - 1.82 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}Δm≈−1.82×10−12kg.

Check. Do not use a negative electron count. The count is positive; the transfer direction and charge sign carry the physical information.

Identical conducting spheres share charge equally: a labeled extension

For two isolated identical metal spheres that touch, conservation gives Qtotal=Q1+Q2Q_{\mathrm{total}} = Q_{1} + Q_{2}Qtotal​=Q1​+Q2​. Symmetry gives equal final charges after they reach equilibrium. Therefore Qfinal,each=Q1+Q22Q_{\mathrm{final,each}}=\frac{Q_1+Q_2}{2}Qfinal,each​=2Q1​+Q2​​.

For +8 nC+ 8\,\mathrm{nC}+8nC and −2 nC- 2\,\mathrm{nC}−2nC, the total is +6 nC+ 6\,\mathrm{nC}+6nC, so each ends with +3 nC+ 3\,\mathrm{nC}+3nC. The initially negative sphere loses enough electrons to become positive. Unequal spheres do not generally share charge equally. Widely separated spherical conductors have equal potentials at equilibrium, giving approximately Q1R1=Q2R2\frac{Q_{1}}{R_{1}} = \frac{Q_{2}}{R_{2}}R1​Q1​​=R2​Q2​​ before disconnection in that ideal model.

Compare electric and gravitational forces without retaining the distance

Source: Primary p. 21. Use Fe=ke2r2F_{e} = \frac{ke^{2}}{r^{2}}Fe​=r2ke2​ and Fg=Gmempr2F_{g} = \frac{Gm_{e} m_{p}}{r^{2}}Fg​=r2Gme​mp​​ for a proton–electron pair.

FeFg=ke2/r2Gmemp/r2=ke2Gmemp≈2.27×1039.\frac{F_e}{F_g}=\frac{ke^2/r^2}{Gm_em_p/r^2} =\frac{ke^2}{Gm_em_p}\approx2.27\times10^{39}.Fg​Fe​​=Gme​mp​/r2ke2/r2​=Gme​mp​ke2​≈2.27×1039.

The squared distance cancels. At r=5.3×10−11 mr = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m}r=5.3×10−11m, Fe≈8.21×10−8 NF_{e} \approx 8.21 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{N}Fe​≈8.21×10−8N and Fg≈3.62×10−47 NF_{g} \approx 3.62 \times 10^{-47}\,\mathrm{N}Fg​≈3.62×10−47N. Both attract. The ratio is enormous even though both formulas have inverse-square distance dependence.

Situational problems: choose the law, then solve

These added practice problems apply the module concepts. They are not copied examination questions. Keep the stated assumptions when you use each result.

Situation 1: Contact between identical conductors

Two identical small conducting spheres carry +8 nC and −2 nC. They touch in isolation and are then separated far enough for the point-charge model. What describes their final interaction?

  1. Conserve charge.
Qtotal=8−2=+6 nCQ_{\mathrm{total}}=8-2=+6\,\mathrm{nC}Qtotal​=8−2=+6nC
  1. Use the identical-sphere condition.
q1′=q2′=62=+3 nCq_1'=q_2'=\frac{6}{2}=+3\,\mathrm{nC}q1′​=q2′​=26​=+3nC

  1. Determine the force type. The separated spheres have charges of the same sign, so their mutual force is repulsive.

  2. Keep the condition. Equal final charges do not follow for arbitrary unequal conductors without further geometric information.

Answer: They repel, with +3 nC on each sphere.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • They attract, retaining +8 nC and −2 nC. — Contact allows charge redistribution.
  • They repel, with +5 nC on each sphere. — This violates conservation of the +6 nC total.
  • They become neutral because opposite signs always cancel completely. — Only equal and opposite total charge would cancel fully.

Situation 2: Zero force with a negative test charge

At a point, two source-charge forces on a nonzero positive test charge cancel. The test charge is replaced by a negative charge of twice the magnitude without changing the sources or position. What is the new net force?

  1. Factor out the test charge.
F⃗net=q∑iE⃗i\vec F_{\mathrm{net}}=q\sum_i\vec E_iFnet​=qi∑​Ei​
  1. Use the original cancellation.
q≠0,F⃗net=0 ⟹ ∑iE⃗i=0q\ne0,\quad\vec F_{\mathrm{net}}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \sum_i\vec E_i=0q=0,Fnet​=0 ⟹ i∑​Ei​=0
  1. Replace the test charge.
F⃗new=(−2q)∑iE⃗i=0\vec F_{\mathrm{new}}=(-2q)\sum_i\vec E_i=0Fnew​=(−2q)i∑​Ei​=0
  1. Separate equilibrium from stability. Zero net force at a point does not by itself establish stable equilibrium.

Answer: Zero.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Twice the original individual source-force magnitude. — You must transform both contributions and add them.
  • Nonzero because a negative test charge cannot have equilibrium. — The source field can be zero for either sign of test charge.
  • Zero only if the source charges also change sign. — The unchanged zero field already gives zero force for any test charge.

Situation 3: Forces in an isolated pair

Two isolated interacting charges have different masses. Their mutual electric forces have equal magnitudes. Which additional conclusion is correct?

  1. Identify the interaction pair.
F⃗12=−F⃗21\vec F_{12}=-\vec F_{21}F12​=−F21​
  1. Apply the separate equations of motion.
a1=F/m1,a2=F/m2a_1=F/m_1,\qquad a_2=F/m_2a1​=F/m1​,a2​=F/m2​
  1. Compare accelerations.
a1a2=m2m1\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{m_2}{m_1}a2​a1​​=m1​m2​​
  1. Do not add forces on different bodies as one target force. The system’s internal-force sum cancels, but each body can accelerate.

Answer: The smaller mass has the larger acceleration magnitude.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • They must have equal acceleration magnitudes. — Equal force does not imply equal acceleration when masses differ.
  • The larger charge must experience the larger force. — The pair interaction has equal and opposite forces.
  • Both acceleration vectors point in the same direction. — The pair forces, and therefore the accelerations, point oppositely.

Situation 4: Superposition with geometry

A student adds the magnitudes of two perpendicular electric forces on a target charge. What correction is necessary?

  1. Draw each source-to-target direction. Charge signs determine attraction or repulsion along each relevant line.

  2. Add components on the target.

Fx=∑iFix,Fy=∑iFiyF_x=\sum_iF_{ix},\qquad F_y=\sum_iF_{iy}Fx​=i∑​Fix​,Fy​=i∑​Fiy​
  1. Recover magnitude and direction.
F=Fx2+Fy2F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}F=Fx2​+Fy2​​
  1. Choose the angle quadrant from both components. A calculator’s inverse tangent alone can lose quadrant information.

Answer: Resolve and add vector components before finding the resultant magnitude.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Subtract the magnitudes because both forces act on one target. — Subtraction needs opposing collinear directions.
  • Multiply the force magnitudes. — That produces the wrong dimensions and is not vector addition.
  • Add the source charges first regardless of their positions. — Different positions can give different force directions and distances.

Situation 5: Grounding sequence in induction

A negative rod is held near an initially neutral conductor connected to ground. The ground connection is removed first, then the rod is moved away. What is the conductor’s final net charge?

  1. Apply the field while grounded. Electrons can flow to the ground because the negative rod repels them.

  2. Disconnect the ground with the rod still present. The conductor is left with an electron deficit.

  3. Remove the rod. Charge redistributes over the conductor without restoring the missing electrons.

  4. Check the alternative sequence. Removing the rod while still grounded would allow charge to return and give a different result.

Answer: Positive.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Negative. — Electrons are repelled out of the conductor during grounding in this arrangement.
  • Necessarily neutral because the rod never touches it. — Grounding permits charge transfer even without rod contact.
  • Its sign depends only on the conductor’s mass. — The transfer sequence, not mass, determines the sign here.

Situation 6: Two perpendicular source forces

A +1.0 nC target is at the origin. A −2.0 nC source is at (0.030 m,0), and a −3.0 nC source is at (0,0.040 m). Find the net-force magnitude on the target. Use k=8.99×109 N m2 C−2k=8.99\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}k=8.99×109Nm2C−2.

  1. Set directions. Both sources attract the positive target: the first force is east, and the second is north.

  2. Calculate the east component.

Fx=k(1.0×10−9)(2.0×10−9)0.0302F_x=\frac{k(1.0\times10^{-9})(2.0\times10^{-9})}{0.030^2}Fx​=0.0302k(1.0×10−9)(2.0×10−9)​
  1. Calculate the north component.
Fy=k(1.0×10−9)(3.0×10−9)0.0402F_y=\frac{k(1.0\times10^{-9})(3.0\times10^{-9})}{0.040^2}Fy​=0.0402k(1.0×10−9)(3.0×10−9)​
  1. Combine perpendicular components. The resultant lies in the northeast quadrant; its magnitude is smaller than the sum of the two positive component magnitudes.
F=Fx2+Fy2F=\sqrt{F_x^2+F_y^2}F=Fx2​+Fy2​​
  1. State the result.
2.6139×10−5 N2.6139\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm N2.6139×10−5N

Answer: 2.6139×10−5 N2.6139\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm N2.6139×10−5N

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 3.6834×10−5 N3.6834\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm N3.6834×10−5N — This adds perpendicular magnitudes as if they were collinear.
  • 3.12153×10−6 N3.12153\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm N3.12153×10−6N — This subtracts perpendicular contributions.
  • 0.026139 N0.026139\,\mathrm N0.026139N — Nanocoulombs must be converted to coulombs before multiplying.

Situation 7: Contact followed by separation

Identical conducting spheres initially carry +8.0 nC and −2.0 nC. They touch in isolation, then their centers are separated by 0.20 m, much larger than their radii. Find the final force magnitude using k=8.99×109 N m2 C−2k=8.99\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}k=8.99×109Nm2C−2.

  1. Conserve the total charge.
Q=+8.0−2.0=+6.0 nCQ=+8.0-2.0=+6.0\,\mathrm{nC}Q=+8.0−2.0=+6.0nC
  1. Share equally between identical spheres.
q1′=q2′=+3.0×10−9 Cq_1'=q_2'=+3.0\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm Cq1′​=q2′​=+3.0×10−9C
  1. Use the final charges and final separation.
F=(8.99×109)(3.0×10−9)2(0.20)2F=\frac{(8.99\times10^9)(3.0\times10^{-9})^2}{(0.20)^2}F=(0.20)2(8.99×109)(3.0×10−9)2​

  1. Interpret the direction. The final charges are both positive, so the force is repulsive.

  2. State the result.

2.02275×10−6 N2.02275\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm N2.02275×10−6N

Answer: 2.02275×10−6 N2.02275\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm N2.02275×10−6N

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 3.596×10−6 N3.596\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm N3.596×10−6N — This uses the original charge product after charge redistribution.
  • 8.091×10−6 N8.091\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm N8.091×10−6N — This puts the complete net charge on each sphere.
  • 4.0455×10−7 N4.0455\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm N4.0455×10−7N — Coulomb’s law uses separation squared.

Situation 8: A cancellation point between like charges

Fixed charges +4.0 nC and +9.0 nC lie at x=0x=0x=0 and x=0.50 mx=0.50\,\mathrm mx=0.50m. A nonzero test charge is placed between them. At what x-coordinate is its net electric force zero?

  1. Identify the allowed cancellation region. Between like charges, the two source forces on a given test charge point oppositely.

  2. Set force magnitudes equal and cancel common factors.

4x2=9(0.50−x)2\frac4{x^2}=\frac9{(0.50-x)^2}x24​=(0.50−x)29​
  1. Take the positive distance square root.
2x=30.50−x\frac2x=\frac3{0.50-x}x2​=0.50−x3​
  1. Solve the linear equation. The point is closer to the smaller +4 nC source, as required.
2(0.50−x)=3x⟹x=0.20 m2(0.50-x)=3x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0.20\,\mathrm m2(0.50−x)=3x⟹x=0.20m
  1. State the result.
0.2 m0.2\,\mathrm m0.2m

Answer: 0.2 m0.2\,\mathrm m0.2m

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 0.25 m0.25\,\mathrm m0.25m — The midpoint cancels equal sources, not these unequal charges.
  • 0.3 m0.3\,\mathrm m0.3m — This reverses which side must be closer to the smaller source.
  • 0.153846 m0.153846\,\mathrm m0.153846m — Force balance involves inverse squares, so the charge ratio must be square-rooted.

Situation 9: Tracking electrons through a transfer

A neutral small object loses 2.0×10102.0\times10^{10}2.0×1010 electrons. It then gains 5.0×1095.0\times10^{9}5.0×109 electrons from another object. Find its final charge. Use e=1.602×10−19 Ce=1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm Ce=1.602×10−19C.

  1. Count the final electron deficit.
Ndeficit=2.0×1010−5.0×109=1.5×1010N_{\mathrm{deficit}}=2.0\times10^{10}-5.0\times10^9=1.5\times10^{10}Ndeficit​=2.0×1010−5.0×109=1.5×1010

  1. Choose the charge sign. The object still has fewer electrons than its neutral state, so its charge is positive.

  2. Multiply the net count by elementary charge. Track the signed net transfer before multiplying; do not add all transfer magnitudes.

Q=+(1.5×1010)(1.602×10−19)Q=+(1.5\times10^{10})(1.602\times10^{-19})Q=+(1.5×1010)(1.602×10−19)
  1. State the result.
2.403×10−9 C2.403\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C2.403×10−9C

Answer: 2.403×10−9 C2.403\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C2.403×10−9C

Why the other answers do not work:

  • −2.403×10−9 C-2.403\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C−2.403×10−9C — An electron deficit gives positive charge.
  • 4.005×10−9 C4.005\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C4.005×10−9C — Returning electrons reduces, rather than increases, the deficit.
  • 3.204×10−9 C3.204\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C3.204×10−9C — This omits the second transfer.

Situation 10: A mutual force and one acceleration

Two isolated small charges +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC are 0.30 m apart. The +2.0 μC body has mass 0.010 kg. Find its initial acceleration magnitude from the electric interaction. Ignore every other force; k=8.99×109 N m2 C−2k=8.99\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}k=8.99×109Nm2C−2.

  1. Find the initial force magnitude.
F=k∣q1q2∣r2F=\frac{k|q_1q_2|}{r^2}F=r2k∣q1​q2​∣​
  1. Convert both microcoulomb values.
F=(8.99×109)(2.0×10−6)(3.0×10−6)0.302F=\frac{(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})(3.0\times10^{-6})}{0.30^2}F=0.302(8.99×109)(2.0×10−6)(3.0×10−6)​
  1. Apply Newton’s second law to the specified body.
a=F0.010a=\frac F{0.010}a=0.010F​

  1. Interpret the instantaneous result. The positive body initially accelerates toward the negative body. The acceleration changes if their separation changes.

  2. State the result.

59.9333 m s−259.9333\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}59.9333ms−2

Answer: 59.9333 m s−259.9333\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}59.9333ms−2

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 0.599333 m s−20.599333\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}0.599333ms−2 — This is a force in newtons, not acceleration.
  • 17.98 m s−217.98\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}17.98ms−2 — The charge separation must be squared.
  • 0.00599333 m s−20.00599333\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}0.00599333ms−2 — Acceleration divides force by mass.

Fx=−K(1+1/(22))=−1.52106×10−5 NF_x=-K(1+1/(2\sqrt2))=-1.52106\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm NFx​=−K(1+1/(22​))=−1.52106×10−5N

Situation 60: Forces from three square corners · model check

A target +q=2×10−9 C+q=2\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm C+q=2×10−9C is at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0). Fixed sources are +Q+Q+Q at (a,0)(a,0)(a,0), −2Q-2Q−2Q at (0,a)(0,a)(0,a), and +Q+Q+Q at (a,a)(a,a)(a,a). Use a=0.08 ma=0.08\,\mathrm ma=0.08m, Q=4×10−9 CQ=4\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm CQ=4×10−9C, and k=8.99×109k=8.99\times10^9k=8.99×109 in SI units. Choose right and upward as positive x and y. What is wrong with using a as the diagonal source-to-target distance?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Add the three forces on the same target. The diagonal source is farther away by a factor of square root two.

  2. Define an adjacent-corner force scale.

K=kqQ/a2=1.12375×10−5 NK=kqQ/a^2=1.12375\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm NK=kqQ/a2=1.12375×10−5N
  1. Resolve the diagonal repulsion.
Fd,x=Fd,y=−K22F_{d,x}=F_{d,y}=-\frac{K}{2\sqrt2}Fd,x​=Fd,y​=−22​K​
  1. Add both Cartesian components.
Fx=−K−K22=−1.52106×10−5,Fy=2K−K22=1.85019×10−5(N)F_x=-K-\frac{K}{2\sqrt2}=-1.52106\times10^{-5},\quad F_y=2K-\frac{K}{2\sqrt2}=1.85019\times10^{-5}\quad(\mathrm N)Fx​=−K−22​K​=−1.52106×10−5,Fy​=2K−22​K​=1.85019×10−5(N)
  1. Apply the conclusion. The component projection then adds another factor of 1/21/\sqrt21/2​.

Answer: The diagonal distance is a2a\sqrt2a2​, so its inverse-square force has an extra factor of one half.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Nothing; every corner of a square is equally far from the origin. — Adjacent and opposite corners have different distances.
  • Only the force direction changes; its magnitude is unaffected. — Coulomb magnitude depends on the squared distance.
  • The diagonal source has zero field by symmetry. — The single diagonal source has a nonzero force contribution.
